record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures superposition, feature dropping, and interference in sparse toy models, and reports that adversarial training reduces superposition by dropping features. Its reported retained-feature geometry is antipodal rather than nearly orthogonal, refining the geometry claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports outcomes for its superposition, representational-power, feature-dropping, interference, and structured-data measurements. Figure-only values are recorded as such. Its stated sparsity cutoffs and chosen sweep are setup rationale, not separate results.
record.test_reason: It trains Elhage-style toy models (100 features, 20 dimensions) across sparsity levels under standard and adversarial training. It reports how many features each model represents in superposition. The standard models bear directly on V1. The adversarial models are a new training setting in which superposition is reduced. Most rows measure the adversarial-versus-standard difference and its mechanism, which V1 does not name.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author claims a causal chain: adversarial training abandons non-robust features, leaving fewer features and so less superposition. The dropped features are said to match the non-robust set exactly. The author also says kept features' near-antipodal interference aligns with Elhage et al., rather than contradicting them. Limits acknowledged are the toy setting and an approximate robust/non-robust taxonomy.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the Elhage-style toy-model setup and sparsity mask, but adds adversarial training, changes the superposition measure, and introduces a structured robust/non-robust dataset and feature-dropping/interference analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported superposition gap widens with increasing sparsity. On structured data, exactly 70 features are dropped by the adversarially trained model at each tested sparsity level; the standard model drops none at S = 0.88 and 0.90.

fits_no_version.finding: The adversarially trained toy model drops exactly the 70 low-amplitude 'non-robust' features at every sparsity level. Dropped features show higher summed interference than kept ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial training reduces toy-model superposition by pruning low-amplitude (non-robust) features. This is confounded with feature importance, because non-robust features carry amplitude 0.2 versus 6.0.

record.peer_reviewed: Accepted at the COLM 2026 Workshop on AI Interpretability (AIW), as stated in the text.
record.problems: The evidence is limited to toy models optimizing reconstruction loss, which the author says falls short of real-world classification. The robust/non-robust taxonomy is an approximation instantiated through chosen amplitudes. The text gives no error bars, significance tests, or stated repetitions; many plotted results have no numerical values in the text.

untested.parts: Near-orthogonality of feature directions, the regular geometry (polytopes, per-feature dimensionality), a phase diagram over importance and sparsity, and any shown data for the sparsity transition. It uses only four sparsity levels, one model size, and a nonstandard Φ measure.
Neuron polysemanticity and the claim that features competing for capacity causes it.
No comparison of one-dimensional with multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Sparsity-dependent representation in both regimes: at S≤0.7 models drop most features, and at S≥0.98 both represent all features. It is stated without data and was treated as setup rationale, but it bears on V1's transition.
Φ for the standard model across S. The text says Φ rises monotonically with sparsity, which bears on V1's sparsity dependence. It is figure-only and has no row.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'challenges' label is dropped. Antipodal packing is part of Elhage's regular geometry, and the paper itself says the result aligns with it. The interference measure (an n×n Gram matrix summed by rows, then averaged with feature-indexed masks) is ill-defined for feature geometry anyway. Φ and P are the same quantity scaled by n. There are no error bars or repeated seeds. This is a single-author workshop paper.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish the general sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry across toy-model settings; it tests a limited sparsity sweep and reports adversarial-versus-standard comparisons. It does not compare alternative feature dimensionalities.
Does not test neuron polysemanticity, dedicated dimensions, or whether feature competition for capacity causes polysemantic neurons.
Does not test whether polysemanticity can arise without capacity pressure.
No LLMs, neuron-level feature spreading, or SAE feature recovery are studied.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Uses feature columns/directions in a toy model but does not compare one-dimensional with multidimensional features.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Standard-trained toy model, structured data, S=0.88 and 0.90
source_check.reason: R25–R26 report no dropped features: all 100 features are represented in 20 dimensions. This supports superposition in the tested setting; a transition and near-orthogonal geometry are not established by these rows.

relationships.condition: Adversarially trained toy models (α=0.5, ℓ2 one-step attack), S=0.78–0.90
relationships.reason: Adversarial training cuts the number of superposed features: exactly 70 of 100 are dropped on structured data, and Φ and represented counts are lower on unstructured data. How much superposition occurs therefore depends on the training objective, although 30 features in 20 dimensions still means some superposition (R1–R12, R21–R24). The unstructured values are figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: On structured data, adversarial training dropped exactly 70 of 100 features, and on unstructured data it lowered Φ and the number of represented features. Still, 30 features in 20 dimensions meant some superposition remained.
